title: Houthis Hit Shaybah and Dammam as Washington Pulls Staff Out of Saudi Arabia
subhead: Drone strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure and a US evacuation order pushed Brent above $111 and WTI near $99. Riyadh says production is unaffected and the Houthis deny the attack, but the war has now spread to the Gulf's eastern oil provinces.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia's Oil Heartland Becomes the Front Line
sections.body:
Drones struck the Shaybah oilfield and Dammam's international airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, according to ING's commodities desk and OilPrice. ING reported that an oil processing plant was the target. Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said production has not been impacted. The US State Department ordered non-emergency US government personnel to leave the kingdom, a step OilPrice notes fed directly into market sentiment.

The attribution is contested. Reuters reported the Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport and Saudi Aramco facilities, disrupting flights and exports, while the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted four drones launched toward the kingdom over the Medina and Eastern regions. The Houthis then issued a denial, saying they had not launched drones toward Medina or conducted any military operation against Saudi Arabia on Wednesday. The two accounts cannot both be fully right; what is not in dispute is that the kingdom is absorbing regular drone attacks on civilian and energy sites.

The commercial impact is already visible outside the oil price. Government agencies in Riyadh told employees to work from home, per AFP, and the Future Investment Initiative — the 'Davos in the Desert' conference scheduled for October 26-29 — has been postponed to 2027. That is a signal about how Riyadh itself is pricing the security risk, not just how traders are.
sections.whyItMatters: Attacks are landing in the Eastern Province rather than on remote border targets, which is where most Saudi export capacity sits. An investment summit cancellation matters as much as a drone interception: it tells you the host government expects the threat to persist.

sections.heading: Prices, and the Freight Bill Behind Them
sections.body:
Brent traded at $111.10 a barrel and WTI at $98.98 early Thursday, both up roughly 2% from Wednesday, per OilPrice pricing. The OPEC basket sat at $111.00 and the Indian basket at $115.60.

Goldman Sachs argued in a note carried by Bloomberg and Zawya that the real inflation is in transport, not the barrel. Average global oil freight has gone from $3 a barrel last year to above $20, and Middle East routes are running at $35 a barrel. Goldman breaks the increase down: a $7 war-risk premium in Hormuz, $4 for higher bunker fuel costs, and $4 for the ship-to-ship transfers now happening in the Gulf of Oman, which tie up tankers on shuttle runs and starve other routes of vessels. Supertanker rates on the Gulf-to-East Asia run topped $1.4 million a day in early October. Goldman's year-end Brent baseline is $90 — a forecast its own analysts concede is now exposed to upside.

Morgan Stanley, via Bloomberg, expects fuel tightness to persist into mid-2027 because refiners deferred maintenance while running flat out. Planned refinery maintenance is set to peak at 3.4 million bpd in Q2 2027 — about two and a half times a normal spring turnaround, and more than the Middle East and Russian capacity currently offline.
sections.whyItMatters: The marginal barrel is no longer scarce in the ground; it is scarce on water. That is why physical flows can look healthy while delivered prices stay high, and why the price falls only when shipping risk falls.

sections.heading: Russia Sends Its First Diesel Cargo to the United States
sections.body:
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters Wednesday that Russia will ship its first diesel tanker to the US on Thursday under the Trump-Putin arrangement. He gave the cargo at 40,000 tons and did not name the port, saying further shipments would follow and that Russia would 'meet the United States' needs, to the extent of our capabilities,' per RIA via Reuters and TASS. Putin told US envoy Steve Witkoff the tanker would depart in two to three days, adding that the 'financial component should be provided,' Reuters reported.

Scale matters here. Trump said on October 9 that Russia would export more than 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that; Moscow partially lifted its diesel export ban on October 10, allowing 500,000 tons in a first stage, per Kommersant. Kpler's Michelle Brouhard calculated that the initial 300,000 tons equals roughly 73,000 bpd over a month — not enough to move a global diesel market where US retail diesel has stayed above $6 a gallon since September.

The political spillover is running ahead of the barrels. Ukraine has complained of disrupted intelligence sharing and limits on Starshield use since the deal, though Zelensky said a meeting with Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday resolved those issues. Meanwhile Russian strikes overnight into Wednesday killed four people and hit energy facilities in the Kyiv, Volyn, Odesa and Mykolaiv regions, according to Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi via Interfax-Ukraine.
sections.whyItMatters: Forty thousand tons is a gesture, not a supply solution. The arrangement's real function is political: it reorders US-Ukraine relations and gives Moscow a seat in Western fuel logistics in exchange for volume it can barely spare.

sections.heading: India and Japan Hedge, and Japan's Numbers Are Brutal
sections.body:
Indian Oil Corporation will trim the share of Middle East crude it buys under annual term deals for fiscal 2027/28, which begins in March, a source told Reuters. IOC had planned to source 47% of its crude from the Middle East and will now 'slightly' reduce that. Indian refiners have already suspended some term purchases and pivoted to Brazil, Venezuela and Ecuador. Middle East producers are responding by offering cargoes at discounts to the Dubai/Oman benchmark and selling on a delivered basis to absorb freight cost — a concession that shows how hard they are fighting for Asian market share. The cost is stark: India's April-September crude import bill hit $90.6 billion, up 46.3% from $61.9 billion, with import volumes flat to lower.

Japan's half-year data, released Wednesday by the Finance Ministry, shows the same effect with even less volume. The trade deficit for April-September reached $17.8 billion, nearly double a year earlier. Petroleum import volume fell 21.2% while value rose 26.3%. LNG volumes fell 8.4% while value rose 13.5%. Japan bought less and paid much more. Before the war, more than 90% of its crude came from the Middle East through Hormuz; it has since drawn on strategic reserves as part of the IEA's 400-million-barrel coordinated release.
sections.whyItMatters: Both responses point the same way: the world's third and fourth largest oil importers are structurally reducing Gulf dependence. That rewriting of trade flows will outlast the war, and Gulf producers' discounts show they know it.

sections.heading: Gulf Barrels Are Flowing — Just Not as Crude or as Products
sections.body:
The underlying supply picture is more resilient than the headlines, and that ambiguity is what traders are struggling with. Kuwait Petroleum Corp's CEO said Kuwait is exporting as much crude as before the war and producing above 2 million bpd, per ING. But he conceded that shipping refined products remains a serious problem, with flows still well below pre-war levels.

Saudi Arabia illustrates the divergence in JODI data reported by Reuters: August crude exports rose 7.9% to 4.451 million bpd, the highest since March, while production fell to a record low of 6.24 million bpd — down from 8.135 million bpd in July and 6.560 million in May. Refinery throughput fell 181,000 bpd to 2.297 million bpd. UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo attributed the export recovery to Saudi Arabia 'leveraging terminals on both coasts.' Kpler data showed Gulf exporters topping pre-war crude export levels on 14 days in September, with Saudi crude and condensate loadings averaging 9.1 million bpd in the week from September 21.

Read the two together and Saudi strategy is clear: draw down stored crude and route through the Red Sea to keep export revenue intact while domestic production is impaired. That is a buffer being spent, not a recovery.
sections.whyItMatters: Crude is getting out; products are not. The bottleneck has migrated downstream, which is why diesel and jet stay expensive even as tanker counts from the Gulf normalize — and why Saudi's record-low production is the number to watch, not its exports.

sections.heading: The Food Crisis Is Now an Energy Story
sections.body:
S&P Global Institute published a report on Monday warning of a 'multidirectional squeeze on world agriculture,' as OilPrice summarised. The mechanism is fertiliser. Before the US and Israeli offensive in Iran began in February, half of all the world's fertiliser feedstock exports passed through the Strait of Hormuz — urea, ammonia, sulfur, hydrogen, natural gas and nitrogen. The IMF projects fertiliser prices up 10% by end-2026, adding 5% to food costs this year and 2.4% in 2027. Diesel is a direct input cost for farmers, and higher biofuel demand pulls acreage away from food.

S&P's key point is that even if Hormuz stays open, Gulf gas output needs months or years to recover. Rystad Energy put the total cost of repairing damaged oil and gas infrastructure at $25 billion, with Qatari and Iranian gas assets the worst hit and slowest to fix.
sections.whyItMatters: Fertiliser, not crude, is where this war reaches the poorest countries — the ones where food is roughly half of household spending. The repair timeline means this cost persists after any ceasefire.

sections.heading: Nickel, Rare Earths and the Transition's Own Chokepoints
sections.body:
LME nickel settled 3.65% higher on coordinated Indonesian production cuts, per ING. Major Chinese producers operating in Indonesia plan to halve output of mixed hydroxide precipitate, a key battery feedstock, and cut nickel pig iron output for stainless by about 20%. A similar proposal failed to reach consensus in August; persistent price weakness brought producers back to the table. This is a supply-management cartel forming outside OPEC's framework, in a metal the energy transition depends on.

On rare earths, Reuters and OilPrice report that when Japan signalled it would not stay neutral in a Taiwan contingency, Beijing sharply restricted heavy rare earth exports including dysprosium and terbium. Washington has set a January 1, 2027 deadline banning Chinese-origin rare earths in US weapons systems, and defence manufacturers are warning the replacement chain will not be ready. The IEA estimates rare earth permanent magnets underpin industries worth about $1.5 trillion annually in the US alone; AP puts weapons depleted in the Iran war at $28 billion.

In the Gulf itself, Emirates Global Aluminium has restored half capacity at its Al Taweelah smelter in Abu Dhabi after war damage, per ING.
sections.whyItMatters: Two separate supply chains — battery metals and defence magnets — are being managed by producer states for political and price reasons at the same moment. The January 2027 deadline is a hard date with no obvious path to compliance.

bottomLine: The war's geographic centre of gravity moved into Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province on Wednesday, and the market reacted by paying more for transport than for the barrel itself — Brent above $111 while Gulf crude keeps flowing at pre-war rates. The contradiction is the story: Saudi exports at a five-month high on record-low production, Kuwait pumping above 2 million bpd while its product exports lag, and a $20-a-barrel global freight bill that no volume of crude can fix. Meanwhile the political economy is fracturing quietly. Russia is sending its first diesel tanker to the US under a deal whose volume is trivial and whose strategic meaning is not. India is trimming Middle East term volumes for 2028 and Japan is importing less and paying a third more. And the war's sharpest downstream consequence is not at the pump but in fertiliser, where half of global feedstock exports used to transit Hormuz and the IMF expects a 10% price rise by year-end. Watch Saudi production, not Saudi exports. Watch refinery maintenance into Q2 2027, when 3.4 million bpd comes offline. And watch whether the Houthi denial of Wednesday's attack holds — if it does not, the Gulf's eastern oil provinces are a permanent target set.
sources: OilPrice.com, ING Think (Commodities Feed), Reuters, Bloomberg, S&P Global Institute, JODI, Kpler, Rystad Energy, Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, IEA, TASS, RIA, Kommersant, Interfax-Ukraine, AFP, Zawya, UBS, LSEG, AP
